title: Open letter: Importance of Wi-Fi® in upper 6 GHz
content:
Dear Minister:
Following on from our recent letter regarding the future of wireless connectivity in Europe, we are writing to raise our profound concerns about how the EU is addressing this important issue. When it comes to allocating key spectrum bands, political considerations appear to be now overriding the concrete evidence gathered by the EU’s expert groups.
The extensive input to both the European Conference of Postal and Telecommunications Administrations (CEPT) and the Radio Spectrum Policy Group (RSPG) has highlighted how Wi-Fi is better placed to use the upper 6 GHz band (6425-7125 MHz) than mobile networks.
Yet we understand that the German government has ignored this input and changed its position to now advocate that all 700 MHz in the band is prioritised for mobile networks. If this stance is adopted at the forthcoming RSPG Plenary on November 12th, the RSPG will be disregarding its mandate to study “the efficient use on a shared basis” of the upper 6 GHz band by licence-exempt technologies, such as Wi-Fi, and mobile networks, such as 5G.
Read full letter

title: Open letter: Importance of Wi-Fi® in upper 6 GHz [PDF]

6 November 2025 
Dear Minister  
Following on from our recent letter regarding the future of wireless connectivity in Europe, we are writing 
to raise our profound concerns about how the EU is addressing this important issue. When it comes to 
allocating key spectrum bands, political considerations appear to be now overriding the concrete evidence 
gathered by the EU’s expert groups.  
The extensive input to both the European Conference of Postal and Telecommunications Administrations 
(CEPT) and the Radio Spectrum Policy Group (RSPG) has highlighted how Wi -Fi is better placed to use 
the upper 6 GHz band (6425-7125 MHz) than mobile networks.  
Yet we understand that the German government has ignored this input and changed its position to now 
advocate that all 700 MHz in the band is prioritised for mobile  networks. If this stance is adopted at the 
forthcoming RSPG Plenary on November 12 th, the RSPG will be disregarding its mandate to study “the 
efficient use on a shared basis” of the upper 6 GHz band by licence -exempt technologies, such as Wi -Fi, 
and mobile networks, such as 5G.    
European stakeholders are calling for more spectrum for Wi-Fi 
Blocking Wi-Fi access to the upper 6 GHz band would be devastating to the future of Wi-Fi technology in 
Europe. This spectrum is uniquely positioned to sustain the evolution of the Wi -Fi ecosystem and enable 
the next generation of digital innovation. 
Reserving this critical spectrum for hypothetical 6G deployments that may never materialise – at the 
expense of advanced 6 GHz Wi -Fi technology that already exists and can deliver tangible connectivity 
benefits to European consumers and businesses – would be a serious misstep. 
Wi-Fi is the most cost-effective and energy-efficient means of delivering broadband connectivity.  Indeed, 
most of the responses to the RSPG consultation, including those from a wide range of European 
stakeholders, called for at least 320 MHz of the upper 6 GHz band to be made available for Wi -Fi. In 
Germany, for example, trade associations, representing several thousand companies, have called for the 
entire band to be made available for Wi-Fi. The RSPG should not ignore this very clear message.  
 
            
http://www.dynamicspectrumalliance.org https://www.wi-fi.org/ 
 
2 
 
Failing to allocate any portion of the upper 6 GHz band to licence -exempt use would contradict the 
Commission’s Mandate, and could seriously undermine the credibility of the institutional process. Such an 
outcome would be inconsistent with the EU objectives of promoting spectrum sharing, competition, 
innovation and broad access to connectivity.  Such a move would be a major setback for Europe’s digital 
economy and ambitions to be competitive in the industries of the future. 
Yours sincerely 
 
 
Martha Suarez 
President, Dynamic Spectrum Alliance 
 
Kevin Robinson 
President and CEO, Wi-Fi Alliance

 Wi-Fi® healthcare use cases  1 
Executive summary 
The integration of Wi-Fi® technology in healthcare environments is transforming patient care, operational efficiency, and 
clinical outcomes. As hospitals and clinics increasingly adopt digital health solutions, the demand for robust, secure, and 
high-performance wireless networks has surged to new heights. This paper explores the current landscape, key 
specifications, and challenges associated with Wi-Fi deployment in healthcare settings. 
Market Overview 
The global healthcare Wi-Fi market is projected to grow significantly. According to a report by Mordor Intelligence, 
the wireless healthcare market — which includes Wi-Fi technologies — is projected to grow from $197 .19 billion USD in 
2025 to $489.64 billion USD by 2030, representing a CAGR of 19.95%1.  This growth is driven by the proliferation of 
connected medical devices, telehealth services, electronic health records (EHRs), and real-time location systems (RTLS). 
Healthcare providers are investing in Wi-Fi 6 and Wi-Fi 6E technologies to support higher device densities, lower latency, 
and improved reliability. 
Key medical device specifications for Wi-Fi use 
Medical devices leveraging Wi-Fi must meet stringent requirements to ensure patient safety and data integrity. Key 
specifications include: 
• Low Latency and High Reliability: critical for real-time monitoring devices such as infusion pumps, patient monitors, 
and ventilators. 
• Mobility: support for the ability of medical devices to seamlessly move throughout the healthcare facility to minimal 
disruption in data continuity (e.g., roaming and connectivity reliability performance).  
• Quality of Service (QoS): prioritization of life-critical data traffic over less urgent communications. 
• Security and compliance: devices must support WPA3™ encryption and comply with HIPAA and FDA cybersecurity 
guidelines. 
• Interference mitigation: devices should operate effectively in environments with high RF noise and multiple 
overlapping networks. 
• Power efficiency: especially important for battery-operated wearable and portable devices. 
• Location: support for the ability to precisely locate medical devices and users of medical equipment.  
Current challenges 
Despite advancements, several challenges hinder optimal Wi-Fi utilization in healthcare: 
• Network congestion: high device density and bandwidth-intensive applications can overwhelm legacy Wi-Fi 
infrastructure. 
• Wireless coexistence: unlicensed operation in a healthcare facility means a broader array of devices can be present 
all operating in the same frequency spectrum using different technologies. 
• Coverage and dead zones: complex building layouts and interference from medical equipment can lead to 
inconsistent connectivity. 
• Device interoperability: lack of standardization across vendors can complicate integration and management. 
• Security risks: increasing attack surfaces due to more connected devices necessitate advanced threat detection and 
response mechanisms. 
 
1 https://www.mordorintelligence.com/industry-reports/global-wireless-healthcare-market-industry 
 
 Wi-Fi® healthcare use cases  2 
• Regulatory compliance: ensuring ongoing compliance with evolving healthcare regulations and standards remains a 
persistent challenge. 
Wi-Fi is a foundational technology for the digital transformation of healthcare. Addressing current limitations through 
strategic infrastructure upgrades, adherence to medical-grade specifications, and robust cybersecurity practices will be 
essential to unlocking its full potential.  
Introduction 
Purpose 
The purpose of this document is to capture Wi-Fi enabled use cases in the healthcare market, which spans from hospital 
to home and everything in between. 
Glossary 
Term Definition 
Electronic Medical Record Electronic medical records (EMRs) are digital versions of patients' paper charts that 
contain their medical and treatment history within a single healthcare provider's 
office. They can be used by authorized staff to manage patient information like 
diagnoses, medications, and allergies, and to improve workflow and patient care. 
Latency The delay in time for data to transfer across the network. 
Long sleep intervals Importance of the device/radio sleeping for longer periods of time to conserve 
battery power (e.g., seconds at a time). 
Low power Importance of low power consumption, particularly for streaming battery-powered 
devices. 
Mobile A mobile medical device will move locations and must remain connected to Wi-Fi 
and continue to be in use while moving (e.g., patient monitor). 
Nomadic A nomadic medical device will move locations but does not need to remain 
connected to Wi-Fi while in transport (e.g., infusion pump).  It will be powered on 
and/or the user will only interact with the device when at its intended location. 
Over-the-Air (OTA) 
provisioning 
It includes, but is not limited to, initial provisioning, subsequent provisioning, and 
decommissioning. 
QoE/QoS Demands on network for application or user experience in terms of WMM or QoS 
levels. 
Reliability The importance of wireless connectivity. Examples would include not dropping 
packets/data, staying connected whenever possible and/or access to spectrum.  
Expected uptime will vary by the application’s need for persistent connectivity. 
Note: There is a direct or potentially inverse relationship between reliability and 
latency. A device may have strong reliability use case needs in that the data is 
 Wi-Fi® healthcare use cases  3 
Term Definition 
important, but not real-time, and can take seconds or even minutes or hours to 
reach its destination.  
Security With respect to medical devices, the use case will drive the need for personal versus 
enterprise-grade security.  Personal grade security may be preferred in some cases 
to minimize packets exchanged (e.g., minimize delays due to EAP exchanges or EAP 
timeouts) during initial connection and roaming events.  Enterprise-grade security 
may be preferred in use cases where connection setup delays are not an issue. 
Service discovery Medical device finding/discovering an inventory of services and/or locations.  
Signal quality Importance of a good signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in relation to a device or use case. 
Stationary A stationary medical device does not move when connected to Wi-Fi.  It is in a fixed 
location throughout its use (e.g., imaging device). 
Throughput (bandwidth) Overall load on the network, which includes differentiation between uplink and 
downlink and shows if there is a dominant component.

 Wi-Fi® healthcare use cases  4 
 
Use Cases 
This section captures the healthcare use cases that would benefit from the use of Wi -Fi technology. It is organized by 
location of use (i.e., in hospital, outside hospital and at home). Future revisions of this whitepaper will expand supported 
use cases. 
In hospital – Clinical 
Patient monitoring 
Patient monitoring is a regular assessment of a patient’s health status using a medical device or devices in close proximity 
to the patient. A real -time patient monitoring system consists of physiological body -worn sensors connected to a bedside 
monitor that forwards the acquired data to a central viewer located within the hospital to an EMR for storage and historical 
review, and/or to a remote viewer that may be located outside of the hospital (i.e., doctor’s smartphone). A hospital would 
perform real -time physiological monitoring of patients throughout the duration of their stay. In all instances, a clinical 
specialist will monitor the real-time physiological data and any clinical alarm limit violations either at the bedside or at another 
location (e.g., central nurse station or remote viewing unit).  
A patient’s clinical acuity will likely vary as they move between the general ward (i.e., sub -acute) to the Intensive Care Unit 
(ICU), emergency room (ER), or operating room (OR). This means that patients can be in various stages of clinical health, 
which leads to different connectivity use models and can be classified in the following ways:  stationary (i.e., fixed location), 
nomadic (i.e., spot-check device), and mobile (i.e., ambulatory patient). 
For a stationary example, a patient in the ICU will be in bed in different states of awareness and considered immobile. A 
bedside patient monitor that is wall -powered will be physically connected to the patient so that clinicians can monitor the 
patient's status (e.g., vital signs) both at the bedside and remotely. The bedside monitor, while stationary, may still be 
connected to the wireless network for remote monitoring to reduce the number of wires at the bedside.  
A mobile example would be a patient who is being monitored, similar to the stationary patient, but will need to be transported 
between departments. The patient will be under supervision via a patient monitor and likely will be moving throughout the 
facility from the general ward to radiology, for example, so the bedside monitor or some other transport patient monitoring 
device will still require wireless connectivity during transport. During transport, the patient will generally be accompanied by 
a clinician, so the criticality of the remote monitoring is not significant, as the data is more for Electronic Medical Records 
(EMR) storage.  
Another mobile example would be when a patient is in the general ward or other sub-acute area. The patient is encouraged 
to be active in terms of getting out of bed and walking but is still requires a patient monitor. In this case, a patient -worn 
monitor or wearable device will stay connected physically to the patient while they are active. The clinical severity is the 
most significant in this use case because a patient may not be in bed during an adverse event and may require nurses to 
locate them before administering emergency treatment. Also, the connectivity use model in this case is the most severe due 
to the mobility aspect. In all patient monitoring instances, there is real-time streaming data that is low bandwidth but requires 
very robust and reliable connectivity, but with mobility, the challenge of roaming or handover events leading to connectivity 
interruptions is severe. 
Use case requirements: 
• Robust and reliable connectivity 
• Low latency, low bandwidth 
• Low power 
 Wi-Fi® healthcare use cases  5 
• Seamless mobility 
• High degree of security 
• Provisioning services 
Vital signs 
A hospital will perform spot-check monitoring of patients for a portion of their stay. A spot-check patient monitoring or 
vital signs monitoring system consists of physiological sensors connected to a vital signs monitor, which forwards the 
acquired data mainly to an EMR for storage and historical review, but in less frequent cases, will also forward data to a 
remote viewer or a central station. The vital signs monitor will move from patient room to patient room as the clinician 
makes their rounds, acquiring vital sign measurements (e.g., temperature, heart rate, blood pressure) but without the real-
time streaming application data flow (i.e., nomadic use case). In between rooms or after a round of measurements, the vital 
signs monitor will require connectivity to the wireless network to either automatically or through manual interaction with 
the clinician send the recently acquired physiological data to the EMR or clinical decision support system. This data is 
generally used for trending information to warn of patient deterioration. In this use case, the clinician will respond to the 
physiological data and any potential alarm limit violations, mainly at the spot check device. 
Use case requirements: 
• Robust and reliable connectivity 
• High degree of security 
• Provisioning services 
Patient video surveillance 
Healthcare organizations have deployed video-based clinical and non-clinical applications throughout the healthcare 
facility. Video helps alleviate problems of access to care, especially in remote geographies, as well as access to specialists, 
such as mental health providers. Physicians utilize video across a broad range of healthcare settings, from routine 
examinations and check-ups to life-threatening diagnoses, such as strokes. Video also serves to instruct patients about 
their required follow-up care after discharge, or for teaching medical students complicated surgical procedures. In short, 
the healthcare industry utilizes video in each of its fundamental forms:  
• Interactive, real-time video 
o Examinations between physicians and their patients 
o Consultations between physicians 
• Broadcast, real-time video 
o Advanced instruction for medical students in classroom settings 
o Remote patient monitoring 
o Patient entertainment systems, i.e., live TV broadcasting 
• Streaming, non-real-time video 
o Post-care instructions for patients prior to discharge and as a reminder upon returning home 
o Patient entertainment systems, i.e., streaming content 
In cases where patients need constant supervision (e.g., suicidal, confused, aggressive, or fall risk), hospitals employ patient 
sitters for patient surveillance. The sitter’s job is to prevent the patient and others from being harmed and to notify medic al 
staff when attention is needed. The cost associated with patient sitters can be burdensome to both a healthcare organization 
that manages the service (i.e., scheduling and staffing) and to a patient or the patient’s family who often incur the service ’s 
charges. Using centralized patient monitoring helps reduce these costs. 
Centralized patient monitoring allows a sitter to remotely monitor multiple at -risk patients. The sitter uses a video console 
that presents live streams from distributed cameras. From the console, a sitter can watch all monitored patients 
 Wi-Fi® healthcare use cases  6 
simultaneously and change the focus to a particular camera to inspect an event. In addition, video analytics software 
facilitates monitoring by watching for events such as falls or the absence of a patient and triggers an alarm for the sitter to 
verify the potential problem and take action. Furthermore, with the introduction of Wi-Fi based sensing, video, or alerts could 
potentially be triggered when Wi-Fi sensing detects that a patient is in the room and/or when that patient begins to move. 
The following shows an example workflow: 
a) An elderly patient suffering from dementia has been identified as both a roaming and fall risk. Round -the-clock 
monitoring is required to ensure her safety. 
b) The patient is assigned to a room that has a Wi -Fi-enabled video camera focused on her bed. The camera sends 
video back to a remote monitoring service. A virtual sitter monitors this patient and others located across various 
facilities. In addition, the wireless video camera also sends its stream to an analytics server that has been set up to 
detect falls as well as the patient leaving the room. 
c) Near the end of the day, the patient becomes confused about her location and condition and decides that she needs 
to get to the store. She rolls out of bed and begins walking away. 
d) As she leaves the camera’s field-of-view, the analytics server detects the patient wandering and sends an alarm to 
the virtual sitter’s console. The sitter’s console displays the alarm and changes the monitor’s view to focus on the 
patient room shown by the wireless camera. 
e) The virtual sitter verifies the problem and immediately contacts the patient’s assigned nurse, warning him that his 
patient has left her room. 
 
Although video has a wide variety of uses and forms in a healthcare setting, its base requirements remain consistent. 
General connectivity must remain stable and have sufficient capacity to support multiple video sessions while still carrying 
other voice and data streams. Video delivery must maintain high integrity and privacy standards per government 
regulations, and delivery mechanisms must assure minimal loss as well as low delay and jitter characteristics for active 
video streams. 
Use case requirements: 
• High signal quality 
• Robust and reliable connectivity 
• Low latency, high bandwidth 
• High degree of security 
• Patient presence or movement detection 
Mobile imaging device 
Medical imaging devices are significant investments in a healthcare facility, and their use is therefore carefully planned to 
maximize utilization. It is not uncommon to see imaging devices used 24/7 in a hospital setting, with patients being 
transported at all hours of the day and night to a fixed imaging suite, or by bringing portable imaging devices to the 
patient’s bedside. Fixed systems are directly connected to the hospital LAN, but portable imaging devices may use a 
mixture of wired (i.e., Ethernet ports in the patient rooms) and Wi-Fi. 
Mobile imaging devices 
The digital output of an imaging session would include the prescribed static images or video, along with other patient data 
relevant to the imaging session. For example, vital signs and recordings of patient physiological triggers synchronized with 
the imaging device are commonly included. When the imaging session is completed, the package of information is 
transmitted to the hospital’s central Picture Archiving and Communication System (PACS) repository. For example, a 3D 
ultrasound echocardiogram session may generate a digital package size up to 500 megabytes, and this file will need to be 
transferred to the PACS reliably in under a few minutes. Minimum throughput speeds are therefore expected to be in the 
 Wi-Fi® healthcare use cases  7 
range of 100 megabits per second or more. This minimum rate is expected to double in the next 5 years as higher-
dimensional imaging becomes more widespread and digital package sizes grow. 
Short-range Wi-Fi for peripherals 
Some imaging devices employ a private, short-range Wi-Fi network for connection to peripherals. Examples would include 
physiological sensors, probes, detectors, remote controls, and HD video displays. The host device contains an embedded 
Wi-Fi access point and controls all aspects of the private network. The peripheral clients are pre-authorized to only 
connect to the host via the private network. Administration of the private network is controlled by the device manufacturer 
and shall be appropriate for the healthcare environment, locality, and expected security threat profile.   
Throughput rates between the host and peripheral are currently on the order of 10-50 megabits per second, but future 
rates of over 1 Gbps are envisioned. Use cases with low data rates below 2 Mbps are assumed to employ Bluetooth for 
simplicity and cost.   
The private, short-range Wi-Fi links are enabled during the imaging session and are turned off at all other times.  The 
peripheral clients are used at a range of a few meters, typically within the same room. The short range is advantageous for 
battery-powered clients since it reduces the radio transmit power required to maintain the link, and the lower transmit 
power subsequently improves coexistence with other Wi-Fi networks. 
The device-to-hospital link use case requires: 
• Robust and reliable connectivity for roaming medical devices 
• Appropriate degree of security for PPI 
The private peripheral link use case requires: 
• Automatic frequency selection to avoid interference with other devices. AFS should implement use/avoid channel 
tables to improve coexistence with Wi-Fi infrastructure. 
• Dynamic RF power levels to minimize interference with other networks and lower power requirements in the 
peripherals 
In hospital service 
Device provisioning 
In a healthcare setting, Wi-Fi medical device provisioning is a carefully managed and sometimes manual process that 
ensures medical devices are securely and reliably connected to the hospital’s wireless network. This process typically 
begins with device registration and authentication, where each device is identified by any combination of its MAC address, 
certificate, and/or other unique credentials and assigned to a specific VLAN or SSID based on its role (e.g., patient 
monitoring, imaging, infusion pumps). In some cases, out-of-band provisioning techniques utilizing other technologies are 
used to pass Wi-Fi credentials to the medical device. Hospitals use a combination of personal-grade and enterprise-grade 
Wi-Fi infrastructure with robust security protocols like WPA3 or 802.1X authentication to ensure that only authorized 
devices can connect. 
Once authenticated, the device is provisioned with the necessary network policies, such as Quality of Service (QoS) 
settings to prioritize critical traffic, and segmentation rules to isolate it from other network segments for security and 
compliance. Many hospitals use, or would like to use, automated provisioning systems integrated with their network 
access control (NAC) and identity management platforms to streamline this process.  
Hospitals, however, face several significant challenges when provisioning medical devices on their Wi-Fi infrastructure. 
These challenges stem from the unique demands of healthcare environments, the critical nature of medical devices, and 
the need for stringent security and compliance. These issues include: 
 Wi-Fi® healthcare use cases  8 
1. Security and compliance 
o HIPAA, HITECH, FDA Cybersecurity Guidance, RED Cybersecurity Resiliency Act,  and other global 
regulations require strict control over patient data and device access. In addition, these specifications and 
regulations are enhanced on a periodic basis. 
o Medical devices often lack modern security features, making them vulnerable to attacks. 
o Ensuring secure authentication (e.g., WPA3, 802.1X) for legacy devices can be difficult. 
2. Device diversity and compatibility 
o Hospitals use a wide range of devices from different vendors, many with proprietary or outdated Wi-Fi 
stacks. 
o Some devices may not support enterprise-grade Wi-Fi security protocols or roaming standards. 
3. Network segmentation and policy enforcement 
o Devices must be placed in the correct VLANs or SSIDs and/or frequency band (e.g., 2.4 GHz for guests, 5 
GHz for hospital staff, and 6 GHz for medical devices) to isolate traffic and apply appropriate policies. 
o Misconfiguration can lead to cross-contamination of data, performance issues, or security breaches. 
4. Roaming and mobility 
o Devices like infusion pumps or portable monitors move between access points. 
o During provisioning, or when receiving updates to provisioning settings, poor roaming performance can 
cause data loss or disconnection, which is critical in patient care. 
5. Visibility and monitoring 
o IT teams need real-time visibility into device status, location, and performance.  
o Many devices lack native support for SNMP, syslog, or telemetry, making monitoring difficult. 
6. Provisioning at scale 
o Large hospitals may have thousands of devices to provision and manage (e.g., initial provisioning, renewal 
of credentials, expiry/revocation of credentials). 
o Manual provisioning is time-consuming and error-prone; automation tools are often needed but may not 
be compatible with all devices. 
Use case requirements: 
• OTA Provisioning 
• High degree of security 
• Robust and reliable connectivity 
• Seamless mobility 
• Quality of experience 
Real-Time Location Services 
Location accuracy is critical to the success of Real-Time Location Services (RTLS) in a healthcare facility. A given use 
case will drive how accurate RTLS needs to be. For example, identifying where a medical device is located may be 
sufficient at the room level. However, when locating a patient that just experienced an adverse event, location accuracy 
must be <1 meter (m) to allow clinicians to quickly locate the affected patient.  
In a large healthcare facility, a patient in the Step-Down (low acuity) Unit is being monitored remotely at a nurse’s station 
for life-threatening arrhythmia events using a Wi-Fi-enabled wearable medical device with integrated Wi-Fi Location™ 
capability. For real-time emergency situations, healthcare facilities utilize a “crash cart” that contains tools and other life-
saving capabilities. The crash cart is also integrated with Wi-Fi Location. 
 Wi-Fi® healthcare use cases  9 
As part of the doctor’s prescribed care, the patient is asked to walk twice a day for 15  to 30 minutes at a time. During one 
of those walks, the patient arrives at a central location where other patients and their family members congregate , such as 
a ward waiting room or cafeteria. Shortly after sitting down, the patient experiences a critical arrhythmia event requiring 
immediate clinical intervention. At the nurse’s station: 
• An alarm sounds indicating the patient’s critical condition 
• The patient’s location, accurate to within 1 m, is highlighted on a separate map display running a location tracking 
application 
• The location of the crash cart, accurate to within 1 m, is also highlighted on the same map 
Since the clinical devices in this healthcare facility are certified for Wi-Fi Location, the clinician has high confidence in the 
accuracy of the location provided. He or she notifies the clinician nearest to the crash cart, asks them to retrieve it, and 
promptly proceeds to the area where the patient is located to administer life-saving care. 
Use case requirements: 
• Robust and reliable connectivity 
• Seamless mobility 
• High degree of security 
• Quality of experience 
In hospital – administrative & guest 
Wayfinding 
A new patient, Sam, is preparing for a visit to their local healthcare facility. Sam would like to know where to park and how 
to get to the right building, floor, and waiting area for their upcoming appointment. 
The healthcare IT department installs multiple APs in a dense manner to support location services. Examples of this would 
include APs toward the corners of the healthcare facility, APs in patient rooms as well as in areas where patients and 
family members would congregate, and outdoor APs in the parking structure. The AP layout is then modeled on the 
healthcare facility floor plan and linked to a wayfinding application deployed for the healthcare facility.  
Upon arrival at the healthcare facility, Sam installs the wayfinding application recommended by the healthcare facility on 
his phone and uses it to access appropriate contextual information (e.g., indoor maps, points-of-interest, etc.). The user 
performs no manual steps to select the correct Wi-Fi network or enter credentials (e.g., avoided through Passpoint® or pre-
association exchanges). The wayfinding application presents a route from the patient’s current position to the patient’s 
appointment with a venue-specific map. The map updates as the user’s location traverses the route and provides other 
contextual information (e.g., nearest restroom, coffee shop, etc.).  
Use case requirements: 
• Robust and reliable connectivity 
• Seamless mobility 
• High degree of security 
• Quality of experience 
• Provisioning services 
Outside hospital 
Cellular – Wi-Fi Hotspot 
Wi-Fi connectivity is pervasive within the home, healthcare facilities, and most buildings in between. In addition, Wi -Fi is 
increasingly common in automobiles and other forms of transport (e.g., trains, planes, buses, etc.) to enable constant 
connectivity for the general patient population. When outside of a building, Wi-Fi connectivity usually requires a Wi-Fi 
 Wi-Fi® healthcare use cases  10 
Hotspot that includes an additional technology (e.g., 5G cellular) to backhaul data from the Wi -Fi-enabled device to its 
intended communication partner. 
Wi-Fi Hotspots can provide connectivity for a variety of scenarios. As patients are preparing for a visit to a healthcare 
facility or coming home after an appointment, they are sometimes provided with a Wi-Fi-enabled wearable monitoring 
device to gather physiologic data to determine their current state of health. For patients who don’t have Wi-Fi natively in 
their home, Wi-Fi Hotspots are occasionally purchased by the end user. They could also be provided by the healthcare 
facility but are still managed by a third-party Internet Service Provider. In the case of the patients being transported via 
emergency services (e.g., ambulance), Wi-Fi Hotspots also play a role by allowing for Wi-Fi-enabled medical devices to 
communicate status back to a healthcare facility. Wi-Fi Hotspots are instrumental to providing connectivity for remote 
monitoring of patients in the home and everywhere between home and healthcare facility.   
Use case needs: 
• Quality of Experience 
• Reliability 
• Latency 
• Security 
At Home 
Telemedicine 
Telemedicine is defined as the ability for a doctor to remotely examine a patient when an in-person visit is not possible 
and/or practical. Telemedicine improves access to general healthcare, particularly in remote locations. As an example, a 
patient in a rural location can still converse with their primary care physician whose office may be an inconvenient distance 
away. Rather than forcing the patient to travel for hours for what may be a fairly routine check-up, they can instead visit a 
local clinic and see their doctor with the aid of a skilled nurse and a video conferencing system. They are thus encouraged 
to keep their appointments because they are no longer burdened with the time and resources traveling would require.  The 
video session facilitates a personal, satisfying encounter between the patient and their doctor. 
The following could be an example workflow: 
a) Sophia recently had surgery. She lives in a rural area in Missouri, but her procedure took place in St. Louis, a 
couple of hundred miles away. 
b) A few days after the procedure, Sophia drives fifteen miles to a local clinic. 
c) Upon her arrival, a nurse places her in an examination room and rolls in a wireless cart that is video -enabled. 
d) The surgeon who operated on Sophia initiates a video call from his office to the clinic. 
e) At the clinic, the wireless cart rings, indicating that the surgeon has placed a call.  
f) The nurse accepts the video call. 
g) Sophia then speaks with her surgeon. 
h) The surgeon asks Sophia how she is doing and makes notes in the EMR regarding her status.  
i) In addition, with the nurse’s help, the surgeon inspects Sophia’s sutures to determine how well she is healing. 
j) The surgeon tells Sophia she is doing well, schedules a follow-up in two weeks, and then ends the video call. 
In addition, telemedicine increases access to specialists. For one health system with dozens of hospitals spread across a 
large geographic area, the specialists are concentrated only in two facilities. Consequently, the sites without specialists 
were unable to diagnose and treat ER patients who were not suffering from any physical maladies yet still needed care. 
The provider solved this problem by implementing a mobile video conferencing system at all its hospitals. When a 
physician determines a mental health evaluation is necessary, the doctor at a remote site places a call to one of the 
facilities with a specialist who can then examine the patient and establish a course of treatment.  
The following shows another example workflow: 
 Wi-Fi® healthcare use cases  11 
a) A patient checks in to the EMR complaining of dizziness and delirium. 
b) The triage nurse interviews the patient, marks him as a potential stroke victim, and assigns him to a room.  
c) A nurse escorts the patient to a room in the ER. 
d) Since no doctor is locally available to assess the patient’s condition, the nurse requests an examination from a 
physician at another hospital located in another state. 
e) The physician acknowledges that she is available. 
f) The nurse wheels a wireless video cart into the patient’s room and calls the physician. 
g) A video call ensues in which the physician interviews the patient. 
h) Near the end of the call, the doctor determines the patient is indeed suffering from a stroke and asks the nurse 
to find an attending physician immediately. 
i) The nurse retrieves a local ER physician who speaks with the remote doctor and then assumes responsibility 
for treating the patient. 
Use case needs: 
• Quality of Experience 
• Reliability 
• Signal Quality 
• Throughput 
• Latency 
• Security 
Home monitoring 
Home monitoring allows someone to monitor their health condition on their own volition or from a doctor’s instruction. The 
person wears one or multiple biometric sensors and/or personal fitness/wellness devices . Some devices are worn for the 
duration of the day, whereas others are worn only for occasions such as fitness or sports activities . These types of devices 
are small and lightweight to minimize the interruption of a person’s physical activity and may even be disposable. The small 
form factor and weight restrictions limit the space available for a battery. The compute and memory resources available limit 
the ability to run complex physiologic data processing.  The small or lack of a display can make it difficult to provision th e 
device directly to connect to the home Wi -Fi network. When taking the above li mitations into consideration, low power 
operations, reliable connectivity, and headless provisioning mechanisms are a requirement. 
In most instances, the data traffic model is episodic with measurements taken periodically, and small amounts of data (e.g., 
1-50k bytes) are sent via wireless connectivity to the Internet, thus can be approximately modeled as a very low duty cycle 
wireless connection. An example is a biometric device taking a measurement once every minute and sending that data 
either at that moment or buffering for a future upload. The impact on the bandwidth of a Wi -Fi AP is minimal in terms of 
capacity needs but can still require near-immediate access to the wireless connection. 
Since the processing power on the wearable device is strictly limited, much of the algorithm and data analytics may be 
performed using a cloud service, smart device, or other online service reachable only through a wireless connection. This 
may require some minimal aspect of real-time responsiveness. For example, the case where analytics may detect a negative 
health effect and wish to alert the user to take action. This dictates a requirement for wireless access up to 24 hours per 
day. Poor wireless coverage can occur where a user may be inhabiting connectivity for extended periods of time can lead 
to situations where clinically relevant alerts or feedback are unknowingly unavailable. 
Use case requirements: 
• Low power 
• Provisioning services 
• Robust and reliable connectivity 
• High degree of security 
 Wi-Fi® healthcare use cases  12 
Aging in place 
Wi-Fi technology can empower elderly individuals by integrating smart devices and systems into their living spaces, 
providing better health monitoring, communication, and overall quality of life. The benefits of this integration are numerous. 
• Enhanced safety and health management through real-time monitoring 
• Increased independence and quality of life with smart home technology  
• Strengthened emotional well-being through social connectivity 
• Reduced burden on caregivers and healthcare systems with proactive, data-driven care 
As an example, an elderly man named Vic lives alone but needs assistance due to mobility challenges and a history of 
hypertension. Wi-Fi-enabled devices and systems are installed in his home to ensure his safety and well-being.  Here are 
several examples of how Wi-Fi-enabled devices could be used. 
1. Health monitoring: 
o Vic wears a Wi-Fi-enabled smartwatch that tracks his heart rate, blood pressure, and sleep patterns. The 
data is transmitted to his healthcare provider in real-time for proactive care. 
o A Wi-Fi-connected fall detection system is installed to notify emergency services and family members 
instantly in case Vic experiences a fall. 
2. Smart home automation: 
o Vic’s home is equipped with Wi-Fi-enabled smart lights and thermostats that adjust automatically based 
on his schedule and preferences. 
o Voice-controlled assistants linked via Wi-Fi help Vic operate appliances, lock doors, and make hands-free 
phone calls without needing physical interaction. 
3. Remote communication & social connection: 
o Wi-Fi facilitates video calls with Vic’s family, friends, and healthcare providers, reducing feelings of 
isolation. 
o Virtual hobby classes are conducted online, allowing Vic to engage in activities like board games or 
photography from his living room. 
4. Medication management: 
o A Wi-Fi-connected pill dispenser alerts Vic when it’s time to take his medication. It sends reminders to his 
phone and notifies his caregiver if doses are missed. 
Using Wi-Fi in elder care can bring transformative benefits, but it does come with challenges. Here are some key 
obstacles: 
1. Connectivity and reliability: 
o Wi-Fi networks may experience outages, weak signals, or interference, especially in rural areas or older 
buildings with thick walls, potentially disrupting critical devices or communications.  
2. Technology adoption: 
o Elderly individuals might find it difficult to understand or operate Wi-Fi-enabled devices, leading to 
frustration or underutilization of the technology. 
3. Cost and support: 
o Implementing and maintaining Wi-Fi-enabled elder care solutions can be expensive, encompassing costs 
for high-speed internet, smart devices, and ongoing technical support.  
 Wi-Fi® healthcare use cases  13 
o Frequent technical issues or software updates may overwhelm both elders and caregivers, requiring 
constant assistance to keep devices operational. 
4. Battery dependency: 
o Many Wi-Fi-enabled devices rely on batteries, which need regular charging or replacement. A forgotten 
battery charge could render essential devices temporarily useless. 
5. Integration challenges: 
o Seamlessly integrating multiple Wi-Fi-connected devices and ensuring interoperability between different 
brands and systems can be complex. 
While these challenges exist, they can often be mitigated with thoughtful planning, education, and investment in reliable 
and user-friendly Wi-Fi systems. 
Use case requirements: 
• Robust and reliable connectivity 
• Low power 
• Provisioning services 
• High degree of security 
Summary 
Wi-Fi is a foundational technology for the digital transformation of patient care and operational efficiency. As hospitals and 
clinics increasingly adopt digital health solutions, the demand for robust, secure, and high -performance wireless networks 
has surged. Addressing current limitations through strategic infrastructure upgrades, adherence to medical-grade 
specifications, and robust cybersecurity practices will be essential to unlocking Wi-Fi’s full potential in healthcare.

title: Episode 89: Access to 6 GHz is essential for Wi-Fi®: a conversation with Dean Bubley of Disruptive…
content:
In today's episode, we sit down with Dean Bubley, Tech Industry Analyst and Futurist with Disruptive Analysis, to discuss the ongoing conversation over the 6 GHz spectrum. Dean breaks down the politics, policy, and potential of 6 GHz, and we discuss why the band is essential for home, enterprise, and industrial Wi-Fi. We also examine the misconceptions around the “5G and 6G race,” and Dean explains how solutions like dynamic spectrum sharing could offer a better path forward. Tune in to discover how preserving the 6 GHz band for Wi-Fi could shape the future of global connectivity.

title: Why 6 GHz Frequency Coordination matters in stadiums and venues
content:
Why 6 GHz Frequency Coordination matters in stadiums and venues
Wi-Fi 6E networks operating in the 6 GHz band introduce interference challenges in venues like stadiums where mobile camera operators also use these frequencies. This has created a need for coordinated spectrum management between Wi-Fi® network operators and itinerant camera users to ensure smooth operation of both systems.
6 GHz interference in stadium deployments
When
Wi-Fi 6E
(6 GHz) networks went live in outdoor stadiums and arenas during the 2024-2025 sports season, interference was reported to
HPE
by universities with in-house cameras, by multiple broadcast TV operators in professional sports venues, and by consultants at FCC standards committee meetings. While mobile camera operators have long used the 6 GHz band with minimal interference, this changed when the FCC approved Wi-Fi use on these same frequencies. Although rules protect existing users — mainly licensed fixed-wireless operators — their activities rarely overlapped because camera operators typically worked at ground level, while incumbents operated high on towers using narrow-beam antennas.
Now that Wi-Fi 6E and
Wi-Fi 7
(and in the future,
Wi-Fi 8
) support the use of 6 GHz with indoor and outdoor operating regulations to protect licensed incumbents, there is a new need for network and camera operators to carefully coordinate frequency usage locally in this shared spectrum to avoid additional interference.
Identifying interference
Mobile camera interference appears to the
Wi-Fi
network operator as “channel-busy” notifications from access points (APs) in range of these cameras. The interference can be very broad - for example, a camera located on the sidelines of a football stadium can affect every AP in the seating bowl, making it hard to detect the physical source. Camera operators and content producers typically monitor their spectrum, but do not recognize the Wi-Fi signals and typically report dropouts and out-of-sync video.
When observed on Wi-Fi scanners, a camera appears as a constant transmitter which may be affecting one or two 20 MHz Wi-Fi channels, depending on what frequency the camera is tuned to. There are a variety of mobile wireless cameras, most of which use 8-10 MHz of occupied channel bandwidth with 1-2 MHz guard band. Planning for the use of two cameras per 20 MHz Wi-Fi channel has proven to work but cannot be guaranteed for all camera models. For example, NFL Pylon cameras and similar specialty cameras may each use 18-20 MHz, requiring proactive frequency coordination.
Camera interference – Spectrum capture
Maximize Wi-Fi channel width benefits
The 6 GHz Wi-Fi band offers many benefits, one of which is the use of much larger channel widths. 20 MHz channels are typically used in legacy 5 GHz Wi-Fi networks, but today 40 MHz or 80 MHz channel widths on 6 GHz are strongly preferred.
5 GHz Throughput - 20 MHz channel-width
6 GHz Throughput - 80 MHz channel-width
There are a limited number of Wi-Fi channels, and in high-density settings, the total system capacity is a function of how many times each channel can be effectively reused – so each Wi-Fi channel that is removed will have a significant impact.
6 GHz Frequency Coordination
When the FCC negotiated the re-purposing of the 6 GHz band, it chose (with industry support) to keep UNII-8 as part of the low-power indoor Wi-Fi spectrum rather than reserving it for itinerant camera operators. Many cameras can be tuned to frequencies right below the beginning of the UNII-5 band, with two 10 MHz channels available for camera operations that will not require any reservation of Wi-Fi channels.
If cameras can't use these frequencies, or if there are more than two cameras, the Wi-Fi network operator should reserve channels using these best practices.
Camera channel assignments and Wi-Fi channel reservations
Use the table below to determine which 10 MHz channels to assign to cameras and to reserve the corresponding Wi-Fi channels. Removing channels from an HPE Aruba Network is done by editing the Regulatory-Domain and disallowing the selected channels.
While not necessarily authorized to operate in UNII-6, if necessary, use the table below to determine which 10 MHz channels to assign to cameras and to reserve the corresponding Wi-Fi channels.
Frequency Coordination recommendations
In addition to the channel assignments listed above, venues could consider the following recommendations before an event:
In settings with cameras, inform the existing frequency coordinator of this new need to work with the Wi-Fi operator well before any big event.
There may be multiple frequency coordinators, depending on the type of event at a venue. There may be an in-house coordinator, who is part of the A/V or Broadcast department, that will coordinate with outside producers as well as a sports league frequency coordinator, like the NFL EFC.
For many customers, the concept of frequency coordination with Wi-Fi is new and may require a new role in the IT organization. It is recommended that you assign this task to a single point of contact and make sure they are familiar with these best practice recommendations.
Add language to contracts and agreements with outside organizations that may use a public venue that identifies the need to coordinate spectrum in 6 GHz and be clear that they are required to do so.
It is important to make Wi-Fi channel reservations to protect certain frequencies for camera operators at least 48 hours before any big event, so the Wi-Fi channel assignment algorithm stabilizes.
Begin to monitor your Wi-Fi networks for interference, particularly during event setup. If quick changes are required to protect video content, use these best practices to reserve Wi-Fi channels – but note that to effectuate the change, the network will reset, and user connectivity will be affected.
The addition of the full 1200 MHz of 6 GHz spectrum to Wi-Fi is a huge advancement that has been achieved by re-purposing specific frequencies while protecting the incumbent users of those frequencies. In addition to following the rules for low-power-indoor and the use of an Automated Frequency Coordination system (AFC) when outdoors, Wi-Fi network operators must now accommodate this small segment of incumbent users and coordinate frequencies together locally, just as operators of other wireless communication networks have for decades using licensed frequencies.

Jeffrey Weaver
Hewlett-Packard Enterprise
Jeffrey Weaver has been with HPE Aruba Networking since 2010 and has a long history in the data networking industry. After serving as a United States Air Force Space Systems Specialist, Jeff worked for many early-stage company’s including 3Com, Wellfleet, FORE Systems, Argon, Cacheflow, RouteScience, Xiplink and Tropos Networks. He was originally hired to support HPE Aruba Networking’s outdoor Wi-Fi initiatives and drive early field activities related to new products and technologies. That position quickly expanded to include other complex Wi-Fi scenarios, which led to his leading HPE Aruba Networking’s large public venue team, which developed deployment and configuration guidance for high-density Wi-Fi networks in stadiums and arenas. Jeff also works with HPE marketing teams to size and scope regional and global sponsorship opportunities and leads one of four HPE Aruba Networking Sustainability Guilds called Tech for Good.
Today, Jeff is a Sr. Director on HPE Networking’s Wireless CTO Team and supports field activities related to emerging technologies like Wi-Fi 6e, Open Locate and Private 5G. His strong customer relationship’s enable real-world testing and utilization of data coming from research in the wireless CTO lab in live networks. He is currently incubating HPE Networking’s Private 5G for Enterprise offerings with the PLM team and will support early customer and partner trials as these new products come to market.
